blocks.text: 1. Scaling Strategies

blocks.alt: A single request is compared against many concurrent requests

blocks.text: Latency Optimization closed by tying optimization effort to what the use case actually expects. Scaling Strategies, growing a RAG system's capacity to handle increasing load, closes out this Production RAG module by shifting focus from one request to many requests at once.
It adds more capacity at exactly the layer that actually runs out first as traffic grows.
2. Scaling Is Different From Optimizing A Single Request
Latency optimization made one request faster.
Scaling instead handles many more requests happening at the same time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concern","What it addresses"],"rows":[["Latency optimization","How fast one single request completes"],["Scaling","How many simultaneous requests the system handles"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Horizontal Versus Vertical Scaling

blocks.alt: Horizontal scaling with more machines is compared against vertical scaling with a bigger machine

blocks.text: Vertical scaling gives one server more resources, while horizontal scaling adds more servers running in parallel.
Horizontal scaling has no hard ceiling the way a single machine eventually does.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Scaling style","How capacity grows"],"rows":[["Vertical","One server gets more resources, up to a ceiling"],["Horizontal","More servers added in parallel, no hard ceiling"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Stateless Request Handling Enables Horizontal Scaling

blocks.alt: A stateless request means any server can handle it

blocks.text: A request handler that stores no per-user state locally can be freely duplicated across many servers.
Any server can handle any request, since none of them hold unique local state.
5. The Vector Database Often Scales Differently Than The Rest

blocks.alt: Application servers scale differently than the vector database

blocks.text: As with choosing a graph storage backend in Graph Construction, the vector database holds real, shared state, unlike the stateless request handlers around it.
Scaling it usually means sharding or replicating the index itself, a different problem than adding more app servers.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Adding ten more stateless application servers, does nothing to scale the underlying vector database itself, which needs its own sharding or replication strategy as a separate concern.

6. Load Balancing Distributes Traffic Across Replicas

blocks.alt: Incoming traffic goes through a load balancer to replica 1 and replica 2

blocks.text: As with rate limiting is the direct fix for noisy neighbors in Rate Limiting, once multiple servers exist, something must decide which server handles each incoming request.
A load balancer spreads traffic evenly so no single replica becomes its own bottleneck.
7. Auto Scaling Responds To Actual Demand

blocks.alt: Low demand keeps few instances while high demand spins up many instances

blocks.text: As with cost optimization can hurt quality if pushed too far in Cost Optimization, running peak capacity at all times wastes money during quiet periods.
Auto scaling adds and removes capacity automatically as real demand actually rises and falls.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Auto scaling that adds server replicas during a traffic spike and removes them once demand drops, avoids paying for peak capacity around the clock, the same cost-conscious instinct in Cost Optimization.

blocks.text: 8. Scaling Exposes Every Earlier Capacity Limit At Once

As with rate limiting protecting downstream costs, not just latency, in Rate Limiting, more servers handling more traffic also means more embedding calls, generation calls, and cache lookups all at once.
Scaling the request layer alone is not enough if every downstream dependency was not scaled to match.
9. Recognizing When Dedicated Scaling Strategy Earns Its Engineering Effort

blocks.alt: Traffic growing significantly points toward a dedicated scaling strategy

blocks.text: A system with real, growing or spiky traffic needs a dedicated scaling strategy.
A system with small, predictable, steady load may run fine on fixed, modest capacity.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simple load balancer distributing requests across stateless replicas with auto scaling based on load.

code.content:
class Replica:
    def __init__(self, replica_id):
        self.replica_id = replica_id
        self.active_requests = 0

replicas = [Replica(1), Replica(2)]

def load_balance(replicas):
    # load balancing distributes traffic across replicas
    least_loaded = min(replicas, key=lambda r: r.active_requests)
    least_loaded.active_requests += 1
    return least_loaded

def auto_scale(replicas, total_load, threshold_per_replica=3):
    # auto scaling responds to actual demand
    needed_replicas = -(-total_load // threshold_per_replica) # ceiling division
    while len(replicas) < needed_replicas:
        new_id = len(replicas) + 1
        replicas.append(Replica(new_id))
        print(f"Scaled up: added replica {new_id}")
    return replicas

incoming_requests = 7
for _ in range(incoming_requests):
    chosen = load_balance(replicas)

print("Load per replica before scaling:")
for r in replicas:
    print(f" Replica {r.replica_id}: {r.active_requests} requests")

replicas = auto_scale(replicas, incoming_requests)
print(f"\nTotal replicas after auto scaling: {len(replicas)}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows requests distributed to the least loaded replica each time, and auto scaling adding a new replica once total load exceeds the per-replica threshold, exactly the load balancing and auto scaling.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing latency optimization for a single request with scaling for many simultaneous requests.
Building stateful request handlers that cannot be freely duplicated across servers.
Scaling application servers while leaving the vector database as an unaddressed bottleneck.
Scaling the request layer without also scaling downstream embedding, generation, and cache capacity.
